newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine 97 fiscal gap seen at $4.5 bln - official.
newsitem.headline: Argentine 97 fiscal gap seen at $4.5 bln - official.

text.p: Argentina's fiscal deficit may reach $4.5 billion in 1997, the government said in a letter of intent to the International Monetary Fund released Tuesday.
That represents a 50 percent increase on the $3.0 billion deficit included in the 1997 budget blueprint that Economy Minister Roque Fernandez sent to Congress last week.

The letter said the deficit could rise to $4.5 billion, or 1.5 percent of gross domestic product, after the expected deficit of the provinces' pension funds transferred to the central government and severance payments to public workers laid off under a government streamlining plan were added.
Last week Fernndez said the 1997 deficit would be only around 1.0 percent of GDP.
The letter of intent for an expected Extended Fund Facility loan also envisages an increase in privatization revenue to $1.2 billion in 1997 from $500 million this year.
The nine-page letter also said the goverment plans to issue $1.0 billion in Treasury bills in 1997 -- half the $2.0 billion planned for 1996.
It reiterated previous estimates of a total 1996 public sector deficit of $5.0 billion according to IMF calculations, or $6.0 billion using Argentine accounting methods.

"The government is carrying out key structural reforms to attain a greater degree of economic efficiency, increase domestic savings and investment, improve employment and production prospects and safeguard the viability of Argentina's balance of payments," the letter to the IMF said.

The fiscal prospects of the cash-strapped provinces is now looking up, and the states are expected to post a combined $300 million surplus in 1997, up from a $1.1 billion deficit seen in 1996 and a $3.0 billion deficit in 1995, it said.

The document said cuts in wages and other cost-reduction measures adopted as part of the nation-wide austerity program in place for several years now, plus the transfer of seven money-losing pension funds to the federal government are contributing to turn figures around.
An expected pickup in economic activity and tax revenue will also help the provinces in 1997, the letter said.
But that does not mean state governments will be able to loosen up the purse strings.

"It will be necessary to continue keeping expenditures under control in order to preserve and intensify the progress achieved over the past few years in terms of adjustment of the provincial finances," the letter said.

During a short visit IMF chief Michel Camdessus last week praised the government's policies, expressed full confidence in the economy and said he would recommend that the Fund's board of directors "give its blessing to the economic goals" and approve a three-year Extended Fund Facility for Argentina.
